frameworks.name: Two-Tiered Affiliate Incentive Structure
frameworks.definition: A layered affiliate reward system with unscalable premium prizes for top performers (e.g., top 10, top 50) and accessible prizes for the long tail (anyone who hits a minimum activation threshold), so both whales and small promoters have meaningful incentive to participate.

frameworks.name: Affiliate Machine: Offer-Page-Promote-Support Loop
frameworks.definition: A four-stage affiliate program build: (1) design the affiliate offer (money, free stuff, or both), (2) build an affiliate sales page explaining prizes and mechanics, (3) promote the program through existing channels, (4) support affiliates with onboarding, attribution tracking, leaderboards, and pre-written collateral.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's $100 Million Leads book launch registered 500,000 people, with approximately one-third of registrations coming from affiliates who referred others for free, not from Hormozi's own paid advertising.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: existing large affiliate base from prior launch

numbers.axis: registration source breakdown for $100M Leads launch

bounded_by: Requires an existing affiliate base from a prior launch to replicate the prior-affiliate re-engagement channel

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the prize offered to affiliates must benefit both the affiliate and their audience simultaneously, not just the affiliate, because affiliates are protective of their goodwill with their own audience and will not hard-close on something that feels extractive.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Affiliates have finite goodwill with their audience; if promoting your offer feels like a withdrawal from that goodwill rather than a deposit, engagement and conversion both drop. Prizes that their audience also wants (e.g., a fireside Q&A session where audience members submit questions through the affiliate's link) make promotion feel like a gift rather than a hard sell.

claims.text: For the $100 Million Money Models launch, Alex Hormozi set the minimum affiliate activation threshold at 10 opt-ins rather than fewer, because the lower the friction to refer someone (opt-in vs. in-person visit), the higher the minimum volume threshold must be to prevent inflation of low-quality referrals.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Low-friction referral actions (opt-in to an email form) are cheap to game; setting the minimum threshold high enough ensures affiliates who qualify have demonstrated genuine audience engagement rather than spamming.

numbers.axis: minimum affiliate activation threshold by referral friction level

claims.text: Alex Hormozi chooses non-monetary affiliate prizes (free experiences, access, content) over cash commissions for his book launches because paying thousands of affiliates via 1099 creates administrative burden disproportionate to the monetary value delivered, and experiential prizes can provide higher perceived value than a small cash percentage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: low-ticket or free product (e.g., book launch)
claims.mechanism: Cash commissions on low-ticket items (e.g., 10% of a free book) produce negligible per-affiliate payouts while generating significant 1099 and accounting overhead. Non-monetary prizes (e.g., exclusive experiences, content access) scale the perceived-value-to-administrative-cost ratio.
bounded_by: For high-ticket products, cash commissions may outperform experiential prizes because the dollar amount becomes meaningful

claims.text: Alex Hormozi provides affiliates with pre-written emails, posts, and ad copy that have already been tested and approved rather than asking them to create their own campaign, because the expected output of most affiliates drops to near-zero when asked to build a campaign from scratch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any affiliate program regardless of niche
claims.mechanism: Creating a marketing campaign is cognitively expensive and unfamiliar for most affiliates; asking them to do it removes them from the pool of participants. Pre-written plug-and-play collateral removes the friction entirely, converting marginal participants into active promoters.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses a real-time public leaderboard as a primary affiliate engagement mechanism, because affiliates who are actively competing want daily feedback on their rank, and that feedback loop drives continued promotional action without additional prompting from the program operator.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: affiliate program with competitive prize tiers
claims.mechanism: Competitors seek rank feedback to know whether their current effort is sufficient; visible rank progress signals encouragement to continue, while visible lag signals urgency to increase effort. The leaderboard converts external prizes into an internally-generated motivation loop.
bounded_by: Leaderboard effect is strongest for affiliates in contention for a prize tier; bottom-quartile participants may disengage once they perceive the gap as insurmountable

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses the same four acquisition channels (warm/cold outreach, free content, paid ads, and referrals) to recruit affiliates as he uses to acquire customers, then turns the same four channels over to the affiliates as their promotional toolkit, creating a self-similar acquisition loop.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business using the core four acquisition channels
claims.mechanism: Teaching affiliates the same channels the operator already knows works eliminates the channel-learning curve and ensures affiliate promotions are executed in proven formats, increasing overall campaign quality.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi shares behind-the-scenes performance data (email open rates, ad conversion rates, winning creatives) exclusively with affiliates as an unstated incentive, because marketers in his audience value learning real campaign mechanics more than they value small cash commissions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: affiliates who are themselves marketers or business owners
creator whose audience has marketing sophistication
bounded_by: Does not apply to consumer-product affiliates (e.g., coupon sites) whose motivation is purely monetary

claims.text: Alex Hormozi treats affiliates as a distinct customer segment with their own offer, sales page, and onboarding process, rather than as a passive distribution network; the affiliate offer must be sold to affiliates the same way a product offer must be sold to end customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for high-value affiliate prizes, the optimal design is something unscalable at the top tier (e.g., an in-person fireside Q&A limited to 10 people), because scarcity of access is what makes the prize compelling enough to motivate elite affiliates with large audiences to compete rather than ignore the program.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: targeting influencers or affiliates with large audiences
claims.mechanism: Large-audience affiliates can access most scalable goods (books, courses, recordings) independently; only access to genuinely scarce, unscalable experiences (limited-seat in-person events, direct Q&A with a high-status person) creates sufficient desire to overcome the opportunity cost of promoting someone else's product.
bounded_by: Unscalable prizes only motivate top-10 or top-50 tier affiliates; long-tail affiliates need scalable prizes achievable with 10-30 referrals

claims.text: Alex Hormozi segments his affiliate promotion strategy into three distinct traffic sources with different email frequency limits: (1) his general email list, emailed twice only to avoid over-promoting the affiliate program vs. the actual product; (2) prior-year affiliates, emailed one to two extra times because they explicitly opted in to affiliate status; (3) new product buyers, offered affiliate sign-up on the post-purchase thank-you page.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator or publisher with an existing email list and prior affiliate base

numbers.axis: affiliate program promotion email frequency by list segment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's prior book launch attracted approximately 30,000 affiliates, and he plans to re-engage all of them for the next launch as a warm re-activation segment, because they already opted in to affiliate status and already experienced the behind-the-scenes format.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creator with prior affiliate launch history

numbers.axis: affiliate base size from prior launch available for re-engagement

bounded_by: Applicable only to businesses with prior affiliate launches; does not apply to first-time affiliate programs

claims.text: Alex Hormozi releases two rounds of affiliate collateral: an initial set of tested creatives at launch, then a second set of winners once real performance data identifies which emails, ads, and posts are outperforming, so affiliates can double down on the highest-converting materials.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: affiliate program running long enough to generate performance data

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies that the term used for the same affiliate concept varies by industry: influencer advertising (physical products), UGC or user-generated content (consumer brands), affiliates (direct response), referrals (brick-and-mortar), centers of influence or COIs (finance), and joint ventures (B2B); the underlying mechanic is identical regardless of label.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that Skool (his community platform) and his software company Prestige Labs derived the majority of their growth from affiliates, making affiliate-channel advertising the dominant growth driver across multiple of his portfolio businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: affiliate share of total growth by business

examples.text: For the $100 Million Money Models book launch, Hormozi designed the top-tier affiliate prize as an in-person fireside Q&A at his headquarters for the top 10 referrers. Affiliates in the ATM niche, for example, would have their audience submit questions in advance, and the affiliate would then ask those questions on their audience's behalf during the live session. This made the prize valuable not just to the affiliate (access to Hormozi) but to the affiliate's audience (niche-specific answers they could not get elsewhere), removing the hard-sell dynamic. Below that, the top 50 get to attend in person for a 3-hour Q&A session and can mingle and network, still a strong prize but a scalable approximation of the top-10 experience. For anyone who hits 10+ opt-ins, they receive an exclusive audiobook of 70+ one-minute profit tactics recorded specifically for affiliates, a shot at winning one of 50 raffle seats at the in-person event, and a recording of the fireside session.

During the $100 Million Leads launch, some of Hormozi's top-performing affiliates were paid media specialists with no organic audience. They took the pre-approved ad creatives Hormozi provided, ran them as paid ads without modification, and used that to crack the top 50 leaderboard. This illustrates that affiliate programs serving diverse promoter types (organic creators, email publishers, paid ad specialists) must provide channel-specific collateral to each group rather than relying on affiliates to figure out their own promotional angle.

After the $100 Million Leads launch, Hormozi's team found that sharing behind-the-scenes campaign performance data (which emails were winning, what the stats were, how ads were converting) with affiliates during the live launch was one of the most popular and cited affiliate benefits. Affiliates who were themselves marketers engaged heavily with this data, treating it as a live case study in campaign execution. This informed his decision to include the same behind-the-scenes access as a formal affiliate benefit in the Money Models launch.

practices.text: Build an affiliate sales page that explicitly lists each prize, what affiliates must do to earn it, and how you will help them do it. Treat this page as a sales page selling the affiliate program itself, not just an informational FAQ.

Give affiliates a custom tracking link immediately upon sign-up and display a real-time public leaderboard, so they can verify attribution is working and see their rank. Send leaderboard updates as frequently as possible during the promotion period.

Provide affiliates with pre-written, pre-approved copy for every channel they might use (email, social posts, paid ads, text messages to groups). Do not ask affiliates to create their own campaign; remove all creative friction.

Segment affiliate outreach by list type: email your general list no more than twice about the affiliate program so you are not cannibalizing attention from your core product launch. Re-engage prior affiliates separately with one to two additional emails. Add an affiliate sign-up CTA to the post-purchase thank-you page for new buyers.

Personally (or through a team member) reach out to top-performing affiliates as they move up the leaderboard to offer additional promotional help; this converts the public competitive incentive into a direct relationship.

Include explicit compliance guidelines in affiliate collateral: require truthful representation, no exaggeration, and factual claims only. This protects brand reputation and ensures all incoming traffic arrives with accurate expectations.

When designing affiliate prizes, spend substantial time (Hormozi spends approximately two days) iterating on the prize structure to ensure it is compelling at every tier, simple to communicate, and beneficial to the affiliate, their audience, and the program operator.
